title: Japan Scraps Mission to Mysterious Object, Limiting Chance to Test Harvard Astrophysicist's Soviet Probe Theory

content:
Japan’s decision to cancel a planned spacecraft rendezvous with the small object 1998 KY26 has removed what Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb describes as the best chance to obtain detailed images of it. Loeb argues that close-up observations could help determine whether the object is an ordinary asteroid or the long-lost Soviet spacecraft Phobos 1. That interpretation remains speculative, and NASA has said its analysis points to natural forces acting on an asteroid.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency had planned for its Hayabusa2 spacecraft to reach 1998 KY26 in 2031. But the agency abandoned the rendezvous after the spacecraft’s last normally functioning main ion engine malfunctioned in mid-August. JAXA reported the decision to the Cabinet Office’s Space Policy Committee on Nov. 16, according to the Yomiuri Shimbun.

JAXA said the spacecraft could not make the required orbital adjustments with the thrust available after engineers combined functioning components from two damaged engines. The agency had already calculated that reaching the object would require an Earth gravity assist. Hayabusa2 will instead be redirected to conduct a flyby of asteroid 2015 BM510 in 2028, the newspaper reported.

Loeb said the cancellation means astronomers are unlikely to get a high-resolution view of 1998 KY26’s surface. From Earth, he said, even powerful observatories such as the James Webb Space Telescope cannot resolve the small, distant object into enough image pixels to reveal surface details.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman recently rejected speculation that 1998 KY26 might be artificial, saying on “Fox & Friends” that he had seen no evidence it was anything other than an asteroid. Loeb disputes that assessment. He has argued that the object’s motion and brightness are unusual and has suggested it could be Phobos 1, a Soviet probe launched toward Mars in 1988 that stopped communicating after a faulty command caused it to shut down.

Loeb said he was surprised that JAXA announced the cancellation shortly after he publicly discussed the theory, noting that the engine problem had been known for months. He estimated the chance that the timing was coincidental at less than 1%, while acknowledging that it could still be a coincidence. JAXA has attributed its decision to the spacecraft’s propulsion limitations; the agency has not suggested that the cancellation was related to Loeb’s claims.

Although a close encounter is no longer planned, Loeb said Webb may still be able to study the object’s heat and chemical characteristics. Measurements of its thermal emission, he said, could help researchers estimate its size and surface temperature and learn more about its composition. So far, observations have detected reflected sunlight.

Loeb has also pointed to the object’s rapid rotation—about once every five minutes—and its reported reflectivity. He said it reflects about half the sunlight that reaches it, compared with roughly 5% for a typical rock or iceberg, making its brightness noteworthy. These characteristics, in his view, warrant further investigation but do not establish that the object is a spacecraft.

NASA has offered a natural explanation for the object’s unusual trajectory. A 2025 orbital study led by the agency’s Center for Near-Earth Object Studies concluded that its path can be explained by solar radiation forces: sunlight and the heat emitted by an object can exert a small push, particularly when the object is not spherical. NASA’s explanation differs from Loeb’s proposal that sunlight reflecting from Phobos 1’s solar panels could account for the movement.

Loeb has argued that if 1998 KY26 were a comet shedding gas, astronomers might expect to see gas or dust around it. He said the absence of an observed tail is one reason he questions a comet-related explanation. NASA’s study, however, concluded that solar radiation acting on the object’s shape could account for its trajectory without requiring hidden comet activity.

The object poses no known threat to Earth, Loeb said. Its orbit takes it around the Sun at distances ranging from a fraction to several times the distance between Earth and the Sun. He also cited the 2018 SpaceX-launched Tesla Roadster, which astronomers briefly cataloged as an asteroid in January 2025 before recognizing it from its known flight path, as an example of how difficult it can be to identify objects in space.

Loeb said upcoming surveys, including those planned by the Rubin Observatory in Chile, could discover many more interstellar objects over the next decade. He argued that researchers should examine such discoveries carefully rather than assume they are all natural bodies. Most scientists’ explanations for 1998 KY26 remain natural, and the proposed connection to Phobos 1 has not been confirmed.
